segments.text: The three-act structure works in a sixty-second video. What has to change is {sq}how long the first act runs.
Aristotle wrote the rule down in the Poetics. {q}A whole is that which has a beginning, a middle, and an end.
Screenwriter Syd Field named the three parts {s}setup, {c}confrontation and {r}resolution.
In a hundred-and-twenty-page script, {p1}act one runs about thirty pages, {p2}act two about sixty, and {p3}act three the rest.
The middle is the longest part, because tension does the work. Paul Zak showed people {v}a short film about a father and his young son, who is dying of cancer.
The version with a dramatic arc {up}raised cortisol and oxytocin. {flat}A flat version, the same two at the zoo, raised neither.
From the viewers' physiology, his team {p}predicted who would donate to charity with eighty-two percent accuracy.
And attention didn't climb in a straight line. {rf}It rose and fell, and {pk}peaked at the climax.
Now scale Field's split to sixty seconds. {q}Act one would take fifteen of them.
TikTok's ad guide says {t3}make your point in the first three seconds, and {t6}hook by six. YouTube's intro metric counts {y30}who is still watching at thirty.
So act one {sq}shrinks to the first few seconds: who this is for, and what's at stake. {t}Act two gets the time it frees up.
Use it to {a}raise one problem, {b}make it harder, and {c}add one more turn before you answer it.
Act three is {r}the answer to the question you opened with. Give it, then stop.
Then open your retention graph. If YouTube marks dips in your first act, it's still too long.

_note: No prompt: the backend prepends it to each segment and Gemini flash-lite reads it aloud.
